name: Belief in reward and punishment after death
plain_explanation: The idea that if good people suffer and bad people prosper in this life, justice must be completed after death, with the virtuous rewarded and the wicked punished.
precise_definition: The doctrine of personal immortality and post-mortem reward/punishment, which Russell says became widely accepted among Jews specifically during the persecution of Antiochus IV, when virtue and martyrdom were not rewarded on earth.
why_it_mattered: It solved a theological problem (theodicy): if Yahweh is just and all-powerful and yet the virtuous are tortured and killed, justice must be reserved for another world.
historical_origin: Widely adopted during the Maccabean persecution (2nd century B.C.); not universal even then, since the Sadducees continued to reject it into the time of Christ.
examples: The martyrdoms recounted in 1 and 4 Maccabees, where victims affirm eternal bliss awaits them and eternal torment awaits their persecutor
competing_positions: The earlier view, reflected in older parts of the Old Testament, that virtue is rewarded and vice punished within this life
influence_on_later_thinkers: Passed into Christianity as a central doctrine and, according to Russell, into the New Testament's concrete, temporal conception of the 'Kingdom of Heaven.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: A direct religious response to the political experience of persecution and defeat.
